question.scenario: A 28-year-old primary school teacher presents to Dubbo Base Hospital with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of breathlessness and wheeze, particularly at night and early morning. She reports symptoms occurring 3-4 times per week, with occasional night waking twice per month. She denies any smoking history but has a family history of atopy. On examination: alert and comfortable at rest. Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6°C. Chest examination reveals good bilateral air entry with occasional expiratory wheeze on forced expiration. Spirometry performed shows FEV1 82% predicted, FVC 88% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.76. Post-bronchodilator testing shows FEV1 improvement of 15% (240mL increase).
question.stem: Which of the following spirometry findings confirms the diagnosis of asthma in this patient?

options.A: FEV1 less than 80% of predicted value
options.B: FVC less than 90% of predicted value
options.C: Post-bronchodilator FEV1 increase of greater than 12% and 200mL
options.D: FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.76 indicating mild airflow limitation

mcqs.explanation: This patient demonstrates classic features of asthma with variable respiratory symptoms and reversible airflow obstruction. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, the diagnosis of asthma is confirmed by demonstrating variable expiratory airflow limitation. The key diagnostic criterion is bronchodilator reversibility: an increase in FEV1 of greater than 12% AND greater than 200mL from baseline after administration of a short-acting bronchodilator (typically salbutamol 400 micrograms). This patient shows a 15% increase (240mL), meeting both criteria. Option A is incorrect because FEV1 of 82% is within normal limits and does not confirm asthma; many asthma patients have normal spirometry between exacerbations. Option B is incorrect as FVC reduction alone is not specific for asthma and the patient's FVC is near normal at 88%. Option D is incorrect because an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.76 is actually normal (normal is ≥0.75-0.80 in adults); a reduced ratio <0.7 suggests obstructive disease but is not specific for asthma. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 emphasises that reversibility testing is essential to distinguish asthma from other causes of airflow obstruction such as early COPD. This patient should be commenced on regular preventer therapy with a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid given the frequency of symptoms exceeding twice per week.
mcqs.summary: Asthma diagnosis requires demonstrating reversible airflow obstruction: post-bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% AND >200mL. An FEV1/FVC ratio ≥0.75 is normal; <0.7 indicates obstruction.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 1.2 - Diagnosis of Asthma in Adults
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Diagnosis and Monitoring (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 42-year-old office administrator presents to Orange Health Service for review of her asthma management. She was diagnosed with asthma 3 years ago and currently uses budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms one inhalation twice daily, and salbutamol 100 micrograms as needed. Over the past 4 weeks, she reports using her salbutamol reliever 4-5 times per week for daytime symptoms, waking at night with cough and wheeze twice per week, and having to limit her normal activities on 3 occasions. She has had one severe exacerbation requiring oral prednisolone in the past 3 months. On examination: appears well. Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C. Chest examination reveals clear lung fields bilaterally with no wheeze. Peak expiratory flow today is 380 L/min (85% of her personal best of 450 L/min).
question.stem: According to the Asthma Control Test (ACT) criteria, how would you classify this patient's asthma control?

options.D: Severe uncontrolled asthma requiring specialist referral

mcqs.explanation: This patient demonstrates poorly controlled asthma based on multiple indicators outlined in the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024. The Asthma Control Test (ACT) is a validated 5-question tool scoring from 5 (poor control) to 25 (complete control). Scores of 20-25 indicate well-controlled asthma, 16-19 indicate partly controlled asthma, and 5-15 indicate poorly controlled asthma. This patient exhibits several markers of poor control: (1) daytime symptoms more than twice per week (she has symptoms 4-5 times per week), (2) nocturnal symptoms more than once per week (she has symptoms twice per week), (3) activity limitation (occurred 3 times in past month), (4) reliever use more than twice per week (using 4-5 times per week), (5) PEF less than 80% of personal best on multiple occasions (currently 85% but likely variable), and (6) one or more severe exacerbations in the past 3 months. These features would result in an ACT score in the poorly controlled range (5-15). Option A is incorrect as her symptoms clearly exceed the criteria for well-controlled asthma. Option B is incorrect because the frequency and severity of symptoms, combined with the recent exacerbation, place her in the poorly controlled rather than partly controlled category. Option D is incorrect as this terminology is not standard ACT classification; however, this patient does warrant treatment escalation and potentially specialist referral if control does not improve with medication adjustment. According to eTG Complete 2024-2025, this patient requires step-up therapy, potentially increasing her ICS-LABA dose or adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) such as tiotropium, with review of inhaler technique and adherence.
mcqs.summary: ACT scores classify asthma control: 20-25 (well-controlled), 16-19 (partly controlled), 5-15 (poorly controlled). Symptoms >2x/week, night waking, activity limitation, and recent exacerbations indicate poor control requiring treatment escalation.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 2.1 - Assessing Asthma Control
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Assessment of Control (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 35-year-old warehouse worker presents to Young District Hospital Emergency Department at 11:00 PM with acute worsening of asthma symptoms over the past 6 hours. He reports progressive breathlessness, chest tightness, and wheeze. He has used his salbutamol inhaler 12 puffs in the past 3 hours with minimal relief. His usual medications include budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily and salbutamol as needed. He has had 2 previous hospital presentations for asthma in the past year. On examination: visibly distressed, unable to complete sentences, preferring to sit upright. Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, RR 32/min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.1°C. Respiratory examination shows widespread expiratory wheeze throughout both lung fields, use of accessory muscles, suprasternal and intercostal recession. Peak expiratory flow 35% of predicted. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.38, PaCO2 38 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L.
question.stem: How would you classify the severity of this asthma exacerbation?

options.A: Moderate asthma exacerbation requiring nebulised bronchodilators and oral corticosteroids
options.B: Severe asthma exacerbation requiring immediate high-dose therapy and close monitoring
options.C: Life-threatening asthma requiring ICU referral and consideration of intubation
options.D: Mild asthma exacerbation suitable for management in primary care setting

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with a severe asthma exacerbation based on criteria defined in the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024. Features of severe asthma include: SpO2 <92% (this patient 89%), tachycardia >110 bpm (HR 124), unable to complete sentences in one breath, accessory muscle use, and peak expiratory flow 33-50% of predicted (this patient 35%). The patient does not yet meet criteria for life-threatening asthma, which includes: SpO2 <90% despite optimal therapy, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, hypotension, or respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35 with elevated PaCO2). This patient's ABG shows pH 7.38 with normal PaCO2 38 mmHg, indicating adequate ventilation at this stage. However, a normal or rising PaCO2 in acute severe asthma is concerning as it may indicate tiring and impending respiratory failure. Option A (moderate exacerbation) is incorrect; moderate features include SpO2 92-95%, talking in phrases, some increase in respiratory rate but no accessory muscle use, and PEF 50-75% predicted - this patient exceeds these thresholds. Option C (life-threatening) is incorrect as the patient does not yet meet these criteria, though close monitoring is essential as severe exacerbations can rapidly deteriorate. Option D is clearly incorrect given the severity of presentation. According to eTG Complete 2024-2025, this patient requires: high-flow oxygen to achieve SpO2 ≥92%, continuous nebulised salbutamol 5mg with ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms, oral prednisolone 50mg or IV hydrocortisone 100mg, and consideration of IV magnesium sulfate 2g if inadequate response. Senior medical review and potential ICU involvement should be arranged given the severity and risk of deterioration.
mcqs.summary: Severe asthma exacerbation features: SpO2 <92%, HR >110, unable to complete sentences, accessory muscle use, PEF 33-50% predicted. Requires immediate aggressive therapy with nebulised bronchodilators, corticosteroids, oxygen, and close monitoring for deterioration.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 4.2 - Acute Asthma in Adults
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Acute Asthma - Emergency Management (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 45-year-old accountant with recently diagnosed asthma attends Wagga Wagga Base Hospital respiratory clinic for development of a written asthma action plan. She reports daytime symptoms 3 times per week and night symptoms once per week. Current spirometry shows FEV1 78% predicted with 18% reversibility post-bronchodilator. She has been commenced on budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily and has salbutamol 100 micrograms for relief. She is a non-smoker with no other medical conditions. On examination today: appears well, vitals normal, chest clear with no wheeze. Peak expiratory flow 420 L/min (this is established as her personal best over 2 weeks of monitoring). She asks what signs should prompt her to seek urgent medical attention.
question.stem: Which of the following features in her written asthma action plan should be designated as requiring urgent medical assessment (red zone)?

options.A: Peak flow 350-380 L/min (80-90% of personal best) with increased symptoms
options.B: Peak flow less than 210 L/min (50% of personal best) or severe breathlessness
options.C: Using salbutamol reliever more than 4 times in a day
options.D: Waking at night with cough or wheeze on 2 consecutive nights

mcqs.explanation: Written asthma action plans are a cornerstone of asthma self-management as outlined in the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024. These plans use a traffic light system (green-yellow-red zones) based on symptoms and peak flow measurements relative to the patient's personal best. The RED ZONE indicates a medical emergency requiring urgent assessment or calling an ambulance, and includes: peak flow less than 50% of personal best (in this case <210 L/min), severe breathlessness, symptoms not improving with reliever medication, reliever needed more frequently than every 4 hours, or difficulty speaking in sentences. Option A describes the YELLOW ZONE (caution): peak flow 50-80% of personal best with increased symptoms, requiring an increase in preventer medication and possibly a course of oral corticosteroids. For this patient, yellow zone would be PEF 210-336 L/min. Option C (using reliever >4 times daily) indicates worsening asthma and suggests moving to yellow zone with treatment escalation, but alone does not constitute red zone unless accompanied by severe symptoms or very low peak flow. Option D (night waking on 2 consecutive nights) indicates poorly controlled asthma requiring review and adjustment of preventer therapy (yellow zone), but is not an emergency. According to eTG Complete 2024-2025, red zone management includes: give 4-8 puffs of salbutamol via spacer every 20 minutes for 1 hour, seek urgent medical help or call an ambulance if no improvement or if severe symptoms are present. All patients with asthma should have a written action plan to recognise deterioration early and implement appropriate treatment escalation.
mcqs.summary: Asthma action plan red zone (emergency): PEF <50% personal best, severe breathlessness, reliever needed more than every 4 hours, difficulty speaking. Requires urgent medical assessment or ambulance. Yellow zone (caution): PEF 50-80% with increased symptoms.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 2.4 - Written Asthma Action Plans
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Self-Management and Action Plans (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 32-year-old retail manager with mild intermittent asthma presents to her GP in Dubbo for review. She experiences asthma symptoms approximately once every 2 weeks, usually triggered by exercise or exposure to cold air. Symptoms typically last 1-2 hours and resolve with rest or occasionally with salbutamol. She has no nocturnal symptoms and her activities are not limited between episodes. She currently uses salbutamol 100 micrograms inhaler as needed. She reports using approximately one 200-dose salbutamol inhaler every 4 months. On examination: appears well, vital signs normal. Respiratory examination reveals clear lung fields bilaterally with no wheeze. Spirometry shows FEV1 94% predicted, FVC 96% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.82. She asks whether her current reliever usage is appropriate.
question.stem: What advice should be given regarding her salbutamol reliever use?

options.A: Current usage is appropriate as symptoms are infrequent and well-controlled with reliever alone
options.B: Reliever overuse is indicated as she is using more than 2 canisters per year, requires preventer therapy
options.C: Should use reliever preventatively before any physical activity to avoid exercise-induced symptoms
options.D: Should switch to combined budesonide-formoterol for both relief and prevention

mcqs.explanation: This patient has mild intermittent asthma with infrequent symptoms (less than twice per week) and no nocturnal symptoms, with normal spirometry between episodes. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, her salbutamol usage is appropriate and does not indicate overuse. She uses one 200-dose inhaler every 4 months, equating to approximately 3 canisters per year or 50 doses per month (less than 2 doses per day on average). The definition of SABA overuse that triggers the need for preventer therapy is using MORE than 2 canisters (200 doses each) in a 12-month period, particularly if symptoms occur more than twice per week. This patient uses 3 canisters yearly but with infrequent symptoms, and the eTG Complete 2024-2025 specifies that preventer therapy (regular inhaled corticosteroid) is recommended when: symptoms occur more than twice per week, OR night-time symptoms occur more than twice per month, OR SABA is needed more than twice per week. This patient does not meet these criteria. Option B is incorrect as it misinterprets the overuse threshold; 3 canisters per year with infrequent symptoms does not mandate preventer therapy. Option C, while pre-exercise SABA can be beneficial for exercise-induced symptoms, is not the primary issue being addressed here. Option D is inappropriate for mild intermittent asthma; budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) is reserved for patients requiring regular preventer therapy with moderate to severe asthma. The patient should be advised to continue SABA as needed for symptom relief, but to seek review if symptoms increase in frequency (more than twice weekly) or if reliever use increases significantly, as this would indicate the need for regular preventer therapy with a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid.
mcqs.summary: SABA overuse requiring preventer therapy: >2 canisters (200 doses each) per year WITH symptoms >2x/week or night symptoms >2x/month. Mild intermittent asthma (<2x/week symptoms) can be managed with reliever alone. Review if frequency increases.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 3.1 - SABA-only Treatment
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - When to Start Preventer Therapy (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 38-year-old primary school teacher presents to Orange Health Service for management of newly diagnosed asthma. She reports daytime symptoms of wheeze and chest tightness 4 times per week, particularly in the mornings, and wakes at night with symptoms approximately once per week. Symptoms are triggered by exercise, cold air, and exposure to chalk dust at school. She has been using salbutamol 100 micrograms inhaler up to 4 times daily with good symptom relief. She is a lifelong non-smoker with no other medical conditions. Spirometry demonstrates FEV1 76% predicted with 16% improvement post-bronchodilator, confirming the diagnosis of asthma. On examination: appears well between episodes. Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air. Chest examination reveals occasional expiratory wheeze.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate first-line preventer therapy for this patient?

options.A: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily)
options.B: Combination low-dose ICS-LABA (budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms twice daily)
options.C: Montelukast 10mg orally at night as monotherapy
options.D: Long-acting beta-agonist (formoterol 12 micrograms twice daily) with salbutamol as needed

mcqs.explanation: This patient has moderate persistent asthma based on symptom frequency (more than twice per week but not daily) and requires initiation of regular preventer therapy. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is the first-line preventer therapy for all patients with asthma requiring regular treatment. Low-dose budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily (or equivalent: beclometasone 200 micrograms BD, fluticasone propionate 100 micrograms BD, or ciclesonide 80-160 micrograms once daily) is appropriate for initial therapy. ICS therapy reduces airway inflammation, improves symptoms, reduces exacerbation risk, and improves lung function. Option B (combination ICS-LABA) is incorrect for first-line therapy in treatment-naive patients; LABA should only be added as step-up therapy if asthma remains uncontrolled on low-dose ICS alone after 4-8 weeks of regular use with good adherence and technique. Starting with combination therapy without trialling ICS alone is not recommended by Australian guidelines. Option C (montelukast monotherapy) is incorrect; leukotriene receptor antagonists have inferior efficacy compared to ICS and are not recommended as sole preventer therapy. Montelukast may be considered as an add-on therapy in patients with allergic rhinitis or aspirin sensitivity, or if ICS is not tolerated. Option D is incorrect and potentially dangerous; LABA should NEVER be used as monotherapy in asthma due to evidence of increased mortality risk without concurrent ICS. The mechanism is that LABA provides symptom relief through bronchodilation but does not address underlying airway inflammation, potentially masking deteriorating asthma. This patient should be started on low-dose ICS, continued on SABA as needed for relief, with review in 4-8 weeks to assess response, adherence, and inhaler technique.
mcqs.summary: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is first-line preventer therapy for asthma. LABA should never be used without ICS (increased mortality risk). Montelukast is inferior to ICS as monotherapy. Start ICS when symptoms occur >2x/week or night symptoms >2x/month.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 3.2 - Starting Preventer Therapy
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Stepwise Management, Step 2 (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 52-year-old bus driver with asthma presents to Wagga Wagga Base Hospital respiratory outpatient clinic for review. He was commenced on low-dose budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily 3 months ago for persistent asthma symptoms. Despite good adherence to this therapy (confirmed by prescription refill records and observed correct inhaler technique), he continues to have daytime symptoms 4-5 times per week requiring salbutamol use, and wakes at night with wheeze approximately twice per week. His Asthma Control Test (ACT) score is 16. Peak expiratory flow monitoring over 2 weeks shows variability of 18% (personal best 480 L/min, lowest reading 394 L/min). He is a non-smoker with no other significant medical history. On examination today: appears well at rest. Vital signs: BP 135/82 mmHg, HR 74 bpm, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals occasional bilateral expiratory wheeze.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's asthma management?

options.A: Increase inhaled corticosteroid to medium dose (budesonide 400 micrograms twice daily)
options.B: Add long-acting beta-agonist to current low-dose ICS (change to budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms twice daily)
options.C: Add montelukast 10mg at night while continuing current ICS dose
options.D: Add long-acting muscarinic antagonist (tiotropium 5 micrograms once daily) to current therapy

mcqs.explanation: This patient has persistent uncontrolled asthma despite 3 months of regular low-dose ICS therapy with confirmed good adherence and correct inhaler technique. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024 stepwise approach, when asthma remains uncontrolled on low-dose ICS (ACT score <20, frequent symptoms, night waking, PEF variability >10-15%), the preferred next step is to ADD a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) while continuing low-dose ICS, typically as a combination inhaler such as budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms twice daily. This approach is superior to simply increasing the ICS dose. Multiple trials have demonstrated that adding LABA to low-dose ICS provides better symptom control, improved lung function, and reduced exacerbations compared to doubling the ICS dose to medium dose. The combination also improves adherence as it reduces pill burden. Option A (increasing to medium-dose ICS) is less effective than adding LABA according to eTG Complete 2024-2025; medium-dose ICS may be considered if LABA is contraindicated or not tolerated. Option C (adding montelukast) is a possible alternative if combination ICS-LABA is not suitable, but is generally less effective than ICS-LABA combination. Montelukast may be particularly useful in patients with concomitant allergic rhinitis or aspirin-sensitive asthma. Option D (adding tiotropium LAMA) is typically reserved for patients who remain uncontrolled on ICS-LABA combination therapy (step 4 of asthma management), not as second-line therapy. The eTG notes that while tiotropium is increasingly used as add-on therapy in severe asthma, the evidence is strongest for ICS-LABA as step-up from ICS monotherapy. This patient should be reviewed in 8-12 weeks to assess response to ICS-LABA, with further step-up (adding LAMA, increasing ICS dose, or specialist referral) if control is not achieved.
mcqs.summary: When asthma is uncontrolled on low-dose ICS with good adherence/technique, ADD LABA (use combination ICS-LABA inhaler) rather than increasing ICS dose. ICS-LABA combination is more effective than medium-dose ICS alone. Review response in 8-12 weeks.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 3.3 - Step-up Therapy: Adding LABA
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Stepwise Management, Step 3 (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 29-year-old veterinary nurse presents to Dubbo Base Hospital allergy and respiratory clinic with difficult-to-control asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Her asthma is currently managed with high-dose ICS-LABA (fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 micrograms twice daily) plus salbutamol as needed. Despite this therapy and good adherence, she continues to have symptoms 3-4 times per week and night waking twice per week. She reports perennial nasal congestion, reduced sense of smell, and thick post-nasal drip. She has no history of urticaria but mentions that she avoids aspirin and NSAIDs as they have previously caused worsening of her breathing. She is a non-smoker. On examination: nasal examination reveals bilateral pale nasal polyps. Chest auscultation shows widespread expiratory wheeze. Spirometry: FEV1 68% predicted with 14% reversibility.
question.stem: Which additional therapy would be most appropriate for this patient's asthma and rhinosinusitis?

options.A: Add tiotropium 5 micrograms once daily via Respimat inhaler
options.C: Increase ICS-LABA to maximum dose (fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 micrograms twice daily - already at this dose)

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with the classic triad of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), also known as Samter's triad: asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and aspirin/NSAID sensitivity. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, montelukast (a leukotriene receptor antagonist) is particularly beneficial as add-on therapy in patients with AERD. The mechanism is that patients with AERD have dysregulated leukotriene metabolism, and montelukast helps control both the asthma and rhinosinusitis symptoms. Clinical trials have demonstrated that montelukast improves asthma control, reduces nasal polyp size, and improves sense of smell in AERD patients. Option A (tiotropium LAMA) is a reasonable add-on therapy for uncontrolled asthma on high-dose ICS-LABA and may eventually be needed, but montelukast is specifically indicated in this clinical context of AERD and would be trialled first. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 notes that both therapies can be used together if needed. Option C is not a viable option as the patient is already on maximum dose ICS-LABA; further increasing ICS dose would mean switching to separate ICS and LABA inhalers, which is generally not recommended. Option D (regular oral prednisolone) should be avoided for long-term management due to significant adverse effects including weight gain, osteoporosis, diabetes, and adrenal suppression. Short courses of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations are appropriate, but maintenance oral steroids are reserved for severe refractory asthma only after all other therapies have been optimised and specialist review obtained. This patient should also be counselled to strictly avoid aspirin and all NSAIDs, use alternative analgesics (paracetamol is safe), consider intranasal corticosteroid spray for rhinosinusitis, and may benefit from referral to an ENT surgeon for consideration of functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) if nasal polyps are significantly symptomatic.
mcqs.summary: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD/Samter's triad): asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity. Montelukast is particularly effective add-on therapy, improving both asthma and rhinosinusitis symptoms. Strictly avoid aspirin/NSAIDs; paracetamol is safe.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 3.7 - Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Special Populations and Phenotypes (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 44-year-old secondary school science teacher presents to Orange Health Service Emergency Department with a severe asthma exacerbation. She has received nebulised salbutamol 5mg and ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms at 0, 20, and 40 minutes, along with supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 at 94%. Despite this therapy, she remains significantly dyspnoeic, speaking in short phrases only. Vital signs after initial treatment: HR 118 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 138/84 mmHg, SpO2 93% on 6L/min oxygen via Hudson mask. Peak flow has improved from 30% to 45% of predicted. She has a past history of 3 previous ICU admissions for life-threatening asthma. The treating doctor is considering administration of systemic corticosteroids.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen for this patient?

options.A: Prednisolone 50mg orally immediately, then continue 50mg daily for 5-7 days
options.B: Dexamethasone 12mg intramuscularly as a single dose
options.D: Budesonide 800 micrograms inhaled twice daily via spacer

mcqs.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are a cornerstone of management in acute asthma exacerbations and should be administered early. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, oral prednisolone 50mg is the preferred route and dose for adults presenting with acute severe or life-threatening asthma. The evidence shows that oral corticosteroids are as effective as intravenous corticosteroids in acute asthma (provided the patient can swallow and is not vomiting), with the advantage of being easier to administer and having fewer side effects. Prednisolone should be given for 5-7 days total; there is no need to taper for short courses under 2 weeks. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 specifies prednisolone 37.5-50mg daily as the standard dose, with 50mg being most commonly used. Option B (dexamethasone 12mg IM single dose) has been studied in acute asthma and may have a role, but is not standard first-line therapy in Australian guidelines; it may be considered in patients who cannot tolerate oral medication or have poor adherence. Option C (hydrocortisone IV) should be reserved for patients unable to take oral therapy (due to severe respiratory distress, vomiting, or impending respiratory arrest), or those not responding to initial therapy. The usual dose is hydrocortisone 100mg IV every 6 hours, but oral prednisolone is preferred if the patient can swallow. Option D (high-dose inhaled corticosteroid) is insufficient in acute severe asthma; while ICS is essential for long-term control, systemic corticosteroids are required to treat the acute inflammatory response in exacerbations. This patient can swallow (speaking in phrases) and is not vomiting, making oral prednisolone the optimal choice. The mechanism of action is to reduce airway inflammation, decrease mucus production, and increase beta-receptor responsiveness. Clinical improvement typically occurs within 4-6 hours. This patient's history of multiple ICU admissions places her at high risk for life-threatening asthma, and she requires close monitoring, early senior involvement, and possible ICU referral if there is inadequate response to therapy.
mcqs.summary: Acute severe asthma requires systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 50mg orally daily for 5-7 days (no taper needed for short courses). Oral route is as effective as IV and preferred if patient can swallow. Give early in exacerbation management alongside bronchodilators.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 4.2 - Systemic Corticosteroids in Acute Asthma
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Acute Asthma - Corticosteroid Therapy (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 26-year-old university student presents to Young District Hospital Emergency Department at 3:00 AM with an acute asthma exacerbation. She reports worsening breathlessness and wheeze over the past 8 hours, with poor response to her salbutamol inhaler at home (has used 16 puffs in the past 4 hours). Known asthma, usually well-controlled on budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily. On examination: sitting upright, speaking in short phrases, appears anxious. Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, RR 26/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.9°C. Respiratory examination reveals diffuse expiratory wheeze throughout both lung fields, mild intercostal recession, no silent areas. Peak expiratory flow 40% of predicted.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate immediate bronchodilator therapy for this patient?

options.A: Salbutamol 12 puffs via metered-dose inhaler with spacer, repeat 6 puffs every 20 minutes
options.B: Continuous nebulised salbutamol 5mg plus ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms
options.C: Intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 micrograms/minute, titrated to response

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with a severe asthma exacerbation (SpO2 90%, speaking in short phrases, tachycardia, tachypnoea, PEF 40% predicted, intercostal recession, poor response to home reliever therapy). According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, the immediate bronchodilator therapy for severe acute asthma in the emergency department setting is continuous nebulised salbutamol 5mg combined with ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms. This combination provides superior bronchodilation compared to beta-agonist alone, with the eTG Complete 2024-2025 noting that the addition of ipratropium to salbutamol reduces hospital admissions and improves lung function in severe exacerbations. Nebulisers deliver higher doses more reliably than metered-dose inhalers in severely dyspnoeic patients. The salbutamol nebulisation should be continuous or repeated every 20 minutes for the first hour, with ipratropium given every 20 minutes for 3 doses initially. Oxygen-driven nebulisation is preferred to achieve target SpO2 ≥92%. Option A (MDI with spacer) is appropriate for mild-moderate exacerbations or in primary care settings where nebulisers may not be immediately available, but in severe ED presentations, nebulised therapy is preferred for more effective drug delivery. The dose (12 puffs) is also insufficient for severe exacerbation - if using MDI, the dose would be higher. Option C (IV salbutamol) is reserved for life-threatening asthma not responding to nebulised therapy, or in patients approaching respiratory failure. It is not first-line therapy due to higher risk of adverse effects (tachycardia, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis). Option D (nebulised adrenaline) is not standard therapy for asthma in Australia; adrenaline (epinephrine) is reserved for anaphylaxis-associated bronchospasm, not asthma exacerbations. This patient should also receive: supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥92%, oral prednisolone 50mg immediately, close monitoring of vital signs and response to therapy, and escalation to senior staff/ICU if inadequate response or deterioration.
mcqs.summary: Severe acute asthma in ED requires continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5mg PLUS ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms (superior to salbutamol alone). Add oxygen to target SpO2 ≥92% and oral prednisolone 50mg. Monitor closely for response and deterioration.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 4.2 - Emergency Department Management of Acute Asthma
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Acute Asthma - Initial Bronchodilator Therapy (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 38-year-old chef is brought to Wagga Wagga Base Hospital Emergency Department by ambulance with life-threatening asthma. He has received 3 doses of nebulised salbutamol 5mg and ipratropium 500 micrograms (at 0, 20, and 40 minutes), supplemental oxygen, and oral prednisolone 50mg. Despite this therapy, he remains in extremis. Current vital signs: HR 136 bpm, RR 34/min, BP 148/92 mmHg, SpO2 88% on 15L oxygen via non-rebreather mask. On examination: drowsy, confused, minimal air entry bilaterally, unable to speak, using all accessory muscles, cyanosis noted. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.28, PaCO2 52 mmHg, PaO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L. ICU team has been called and is on their way.
question.stem: While awaiting ICU arrival, what is the most appropriate additional immediate therapy?

options.C: Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5mg/kg over 30 minutes

mcqs.explanation: This patient has life-threatening asthma with markers of imminent respiratory arrest: altered consciousness (drowsy, confused), respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 52 - indicating hypoventilation despite tachypnoea), severe hypoxaemia despite high-flow oxygen (PaO2 56 mmHg on 15L O2), silent chest (minimal air entry), cyanosis, and exhaustion. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, intravenous magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes is recommended as adjunct therapy in severe asthma that has not responded adequately to initial bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Magnesium acts as a bronchodilator by relaxing smooth muscle through inhibition of calcium influx, and has been shown in meta-analyses to reduce hospital admissions and improve lung function in severe exacerbations. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 specifies magnesium sulfate 2g IV over 20 minutes, noting it is safe and can be repeated once if necessary. Option B (subcutaneous adrenaline) is not routinely used in asthma exacerbations in Australia; it may be considered in extreme circumstances but evidence is limited and risks include arrhythmias and myocardial ischaemia. It is primarily indicated for anaphylaxis. Option C (aminophylline) has limited evidence in acute asthma and is associated with significant adverse effects including arrhythmias, seizures, and vomiting. The National Asthma Council guidelines note that aminophylline is no longer routinely recommended and should only be considered under specialist supervision if all other therapies have failed. Option D (non-invasive ventilation) is controversial in acute severe asthma; while it may be considered in specific circumstances under ICU guidance, it can worsen air trapping and increase risk of pneumothorax. This patient is approaching the need for intubation and invasive ventilation. Immediate priorities are: IV magnesium sulfate, preparation for intubation (difficult in asthma - requires senior anaesthetist/intensivist), continued nebulised bronchodilators, and urgent ICU transfer. Consider IV salbutamol infusion if available. The patient requires one-to-one nursing, continuous monitoring, and preparation for potential cardiac arrest.
mcqs.summary: Life-threatening asthma (altered consciousness, silent chest, respiratory acidosis, severe hypoxaemia, cyanosis) requires IV magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes as adjunct therapy. Prepare for intubation, continue bronchodilators, urgent ICU involvement. Aminophylline no longer routinely recommended due to adverse effects.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 4.3 - Life-Threatening Asthma and ICU Management
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Acute Asthma - Adjunct Therapies in Severe Exacerbations (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 32-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant presents to Dubbo Base Hospital antenatal clinic concerned about her asthma management during pregnancy. She has moderate persistent asthma, currently using budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily and salbutamol as needed. Her asthma has been well-controlled for the past year with no exacerbations. She is worried about the effects of her asthma medications on the developing baby and is considering stopping all treatment. She reports she has been using salbutamol approximately twice per week, has no nocturnal symptoms, and her peak flow readings have been stable at 90-95% of her pre-pregnancy best. On examination: appears well, vital signs normal, chest clear to auscultation.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her asthma medications during pregnancy?

options.A: Continue current medications - budesonide and salbutamol are safe in pregnancy and good asthma control is essential
options.B: Stop inhaled corticosteroid and rely on salbutamol reliever only to minimize fetal exposure
options.C: Switch from budesonide to oral prednisolone as it is safer in pregnancy
options.D: Reduce budesonide dose by half to minimize potential risks while maintaining some anti-inflammatory effect

mcqs.explanation: Maintaining good asthma control during pregnancy is crucial for both maternal and fetal health. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, pregnant women should continue their regular asthma medications, as the risks of poorly controlled asthma (maternal hypoxaemia, pre-eclampsia, low birth weight, preterm delivery, perinatal mortality) far outweigh any theoretical medication risks. Budesonide is classified as Pregnancy Category A in Australia (drugs which have been taken by a large number of pregnant women and women of childbearing age without any proven increase in frequency of malformations or other direct or indirect harmful effects on the fetus) and is the preferred inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy due to the most extensive safety data. Salbutamol is also Pregnancy Category A and safe for use during pregnancy. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 emphasises that asthma treatment should not be reduced or stopped during pregnancy, as uncontrolled asthma poses significantly greater risks than the medications. Option B (stopping ICS) is incorrect and potentially dangerous; relying on reliever-only therapy would leave underlying inflammation uncontrolled, increasing the risk of exacerbations which can cause fetal hypoxia. The principle 'it is safer for pregnant women with asthma to be treated with asthma medications than for them to have asthma symptoms and exacerbations' is central to Australian guidelines. Option C is incorrect; oral prednisolone has higher systemic absorption and greater maternal side effects compared to inhaled corticosteroids. While oral steroids are used when necessary for exacerbations or severe asthma, they are not preferred for maintenance therapy. Option D is incorrect as reducing effective therapy without clinical indication risks loss of asthma control. This patient should be reassured, encouraged to continue her current regimen, monitored regularly throughout pregnancy (as asthma can improve, worsen, or remain stable during pregnancy in roughly equal proportions), and reminded of the importance of adherence to prevent exacerbations. Her salbutamol use of twice weekly with no night symptoms indicates good control.
mcqs.summary: Asthma medications should be continued during pregnancy - good asthma control is more important than theoretical medication risks. Budesonide and salbutamol are both Pregnancy Category A (safest category) and preferred agents. Uncontrolled asthma poses serious maternal-fetal risks including hypoxia and preterm delivery.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 5.4 - Asthma in Pregnancy
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma in Pregnancy - Safety of Medications (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 24-year-old semi-professional football player presents to Orange Health Service sports medicine clinic with a 6-month history of cough, chest tightness, and wheeze occurring specifically during and after training sessions and matches. Symptoms typically begin 5-10 minutes into vigorous exercise and can persist for 30-60 minutes post-exercise. He has no symptoms at rest or during non-exercise periods. He denies night-time symptoms and has no history of atopy or allergic rhinitis. He does not smoke. On examination today at rest: appears fit and well, vital signs normal, chest clear to auscultation, no wheeze. Spirometry at rest shows FEV1 96% predicted, FVC 98% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84 (all normal). Peak flow monitoring over 2 weeks shows no significant variability (all readings 95-100% of personal best).
question.stem: What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient's exercise-induced symptoms?

options.A: Salbutamol 200 micrograms (2 puffs) inhaled 15-20 minutes before exercise
options.B: Regular inhaled corticosteroid (budesonide 400 micrograms twice daily) regardless of exercise timing
options.C: Exercise challenge test with pre- and post-exercise spirometry to confirm diagnosis
options.D: Advise avoiding vigorous exercise and consider alternative lower-intensity activities

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with classic exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), characterized by respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, chest tightness, breathlessness) that occur during or shortly after vigorous exercise in an individual with otherwise minimal symptoms. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, pre-exercise bronchodilator therapy is the first-line management for exercise-induced symptoms. Salbutamol 200 micrograms (2 puffs) inhaled via metered-dose inhaler with spacer 15-20 minutes before exercise provides effective protection for 2-4 hours in the majority of patients. The mechanism is bronchodilation preventing exercise-induced airway narrowing. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 confirms this approach for isolated exercise-induced symptoms. While Option C (exercise challenge testing) could confirm the diagnosis of EIB, it is not necessary before initiating treatment in a patient with a clear clinical history; exercise challenge is typically reserved for elite athletes requiring definitive diagnosis for competition purposes, or when the diagnosis is uncertain. The history here is characteristic enough to proceed with empirical treatment. Option B (regular ICS) is appropriate if the patient has symptoms outside of exercise (more than twice weekly) or if pre-exercise SABA alone is insufficient to control symptoms. In this case, with symptoms strictly exercise-related and no baseline asthma, pre-exercise SABA is the recommended first-line approach. If symptoms persist despite pre-exercise SABA, then regular low-dose ICS would be the next step. Option D (avoiding exercise) is inappropriate; with proper management using pre-exercise bronchodilator, most patients with EIB can participate fully in sports and physical activity. Exercise should be encouraged for general health. This patient should also be advised on warm-up techniques (gradual warm-up can induce a refractory period reducing EIB), and to use salbutamol as rescue therapy if breakthrough symptoms occur during exercise. If symptoms occur frequently despite optimal SABA use, or if symptoms develop at other times, this would indicate a need for regular preventer therapy with ICS.
mcqs.summary: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (symptoms only with exercise): first-line treatment is pre-exercise salbutamol 200 micrograms 15-20 minutes before activity (protective for 2-4 hours). If inadequate control, add regular ICS. Encourage continued exercise with proper management rather than activity avoidance.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 5.3 - Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Exercise-Induced Symptoms (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 36-year-old baker presents to Wagga Wagga Base Hospital occupational health clinic with a 12-month history of work-related respiratory symptoms. He reports progressive breathlessness, wheeze, chest tightness, and nasal congestion that worsen during his work shifts, particularly when handling flour and mixing dough. Symptoms improve significantly during weekends and holidays but return within hours of recommencing work. He has no previous history of asthma or atopy. He has worked as a baker for 8 years, with symptom onset 12 months ago coinciding with increased exposure to a new type of enzyme-containing flour improver. On examination today (has been off work for 3 days): appears well, vital signs normal, chest clear. Spirometry shows FEV1 88% predicted, FVC 92% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.81. Peak flow diary from last working week shows significant variability (readings drop from 500 L/min in the morning to 380 L/min by end of work shift).
question.stem: What is the most important next step in management of this suspected occupational asthma?

options.A: Commence regular inhaled corticosteroid and continue current employment with medication management
options.B: Perform serial peak flow measurements at work and away from work to document work-related variability
options.C: Arrange immediate permanent cessation of all flour exposure and consider career change
options.D: Refer for immunological testing (specific IgE to flour and enzyme allergens) and bronchial provocation challenge

mcqs.explanation: This patient presents with features highly suggestive of occupational asthma: adult-onset asthma temporally related to workplace exposure (flour and enzymes in bakery work are well-recognized causes), symptom pattern improving away from work (weekends, holidays) and worsening with work exposure, and documented peak flow variability during working periods. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, confirming the diagnosis of occupational asthma is crucial as it has major implications for the patient's livelihood and requires specific management including possible workplace modification or job change. The key diagnostic tool is serial peak flow monitoring, with measurements taken at least 4 times daily (on waking, during work, after work, before bed) for at least 2 weeks at work and 2 weeks away from work. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 specifies that documenting work-related changes in peak flow (typically >20% variability between work and non-work periods, or progressive decline during working week with recovery during time off) provides strong objective evidence for occupational asthma. This should be the immediate next step before making major decisions about treatment or employment. Option A is inappropriate as continuing exposure to a causative agent in occupational asthma can lead to permanent irreversible airway damage; sensitized individuals should minimize or eliminate further exposure once the diagnosis is confirmed. Simply treating with ICS while continuing exposure is suboptimal management. Option C is premature; while removal from exposure may ultimately be necessary, definitive diagnosis should be established first through objective testing (serial peak flows, and possibly specific IgE or bronchial challenge as in option D), as incorrectly diagnosing occupational asthma could unnecessarily end a career. Option D (immunological testing and bronchial challenge) may be helpful but is typically arranged after peak flow monitoring confirms work-related variability. These tests are more specialized and may not be readily available; peak flow monitoring is accessible and practical. This patient should also be advised on his rights regarding workers' compensation, and referral to a respiratory or occupational medicine specialist should be considered for further assessment and management planning.
mcqs.summary: Suspected occupational asthma requires objective documentation: serial peak flow measurements (4x daily) for 2 weeks at work and 2 weeks away from work showing >20% variability confirms diagnosis. Early diagnosis crucial as continued exposure can cause permanent damage. Consider removal from exposure once confirmed.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 5.6 - Occupational Asthma
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - Work-Related Asthma (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 48-year-old accountant with known asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis presents to Dubbo Base Hospital Emergency Department with sudden onset severe asthma 30 minutes after taking ibuprofen 400mg for a headache. She reports that approximately 5 years ago she had a similar episode after taking aspirin but was not formally tested. She has bilateral nasal polyps diagnosed on previous nasal endoscopy. Her regular asthma medications are fluticasone-salmeterol 250/25 micrograms twice daily and salbutamol as needed. On examination: moderate respiratory distress, speaking in short phrases. Vital signs: HR 108 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 135/85 mmHg, SpO2 91% on room air. Widespread bilateral expiratory wheeze throughout lung fields. Peak flow 45% of personal best. Treatment is commenced with nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, oxygen, and oral prednisolone 50mg.
question.stem: After this acute episode is managed, what is the most important long-term advice for this patient?

options.A: Avoid all NSAIDs including aspirin; paracetamol and opioids are safe alternatives for analgesia
options.B: Undergo aspirin desensitization therapy to allow future use of aspirin and NSAIDs
options.C: Take oral antihistamines prophylactically before using any aspirin or NSAID products
options.D: Aspirin and NSAIDs can be safely used if taken with food and adequate hydration

mcqs.explanation: This patient has aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), also known as Samter's triad or NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease (NERD), characterized by the triad of asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and hypersensitivity reactions to aspirin and other NSAIDs. According to the National Asthma Council Australia Asthma Handbook 2024, the cornerstone of management for AERD is strict avoidance of all aspirin-containing products and all NSAIDs (including COX-1 and non-selective COX-2 inhibitors such as ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, and ketorolac). The mechanism is related to inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), leading to dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism with overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes, causing bronchoconstriction and inflammation. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is safe in therapeutic doses (<1000mg single dose, <4000mg daily) as it has minimal COX-1 inhibition, though some patients may react to higher doses. Opioid analgesics are also safe alternatives. Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) may be safer but should only be used under specialist supervision after assessment of individual risk. Option B (aspirin desensitization) is a specialized intervention that may be considered in select patients, particularly those requiring long-term aspirin for cardiovascular disease, or those with severe nasal polyposis. Desensitization involves gradually increasing aspirin doses under controlled conditions, inducing temporary tolerance that must be maintained with daily aspirin. This is performed only in specialist centres and is not first-line management. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 notes that desensitization does not cure AERD and patients will lose tolerance if aspirin is discontinued. Option C is incorrect; antihistamines do not prevent NSAID-induced bronchospasm in AERD, as the reaction is not IgE-mediated. Option D is dangerous and incorrect; taking NSAIDs with food does not prevent respiratory reactions in AERD patients. This patient should be provided with written information listing medications to avoid, advised to check all over-the-counter medications (many cold/flu preparations contain aspirin or NSAIDs), and to inform all healthcare providers of the AERD diagnosis. Medical alert identification may be advisable. She should also be offered montelukast as add-on therapy, which can help control both asthma and sinonasal symptoms in AERD.
mcqs.summary: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD): asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin/NSAID hypersensitivity. STRICT avoidance of all aspirin and NSAIDs is essential (can cause severe bronchospasm). Paracetamol and opioids are safe. Check all OTC medications for hidden aspirin/NSAIDs. Montelukast is beneficial add-on therapy.
citations: National Asthma Council Australia - Asthma Handbook 2024: Section 3.7 - Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD)
eTG Complete - Respiratory: Asthma - NSAID-Induced Asthma (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 62-year-old retired coal miner presents to Orange Health Service respiratory clinic for investigation of progressive breathlessness over the past 2 years. He reports dyspnoea on moderate exertion (walking up one flight of stairs), chronic productive cough with white sputum most days, and reduced exercise tolerance. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history (ceased smoking 6 months ago). He denies significant asthma history, childhood respiratory problems, or family history of lung disease. On examination: appears comfortable at rest. Vital signs: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 16/min, SpO2 94% on room air. Respiratory examination reveals reduced chest expansion, hyperresonant percussion note bilaterally, quiet breath sounds with prolonged expiratory phase, no wheeze currently. Spirometry performed shows: FEV1 1.8L (58% predicted), FVC 3.2L (78% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.56. Post-bronchodilator spirometry (20 minutes after salbutamol 400 micrograms): FEV1 1.9L (61% predicted), FVC 3.3L (80% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.58.
question.stem: Which spirometric finding confirms the diagnosis of COPD in this patient?

options.A: FEV1 less than 80% of predicted value indicating airflow limitation
options.B: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.70 confirming fixed airflow obstruction
options.C: FVC reduction to 78% of predicted indicating restrictive lung disease
options.D: Improvement in FEV1 of 100mL post-bronchodilator indicating partially reversible disease

mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis of COPD is confirmed by demonstrating persistent airflow limitation on spirometry. According to the COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD management) 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, the diagnostic criterion is a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.70 in the appropriate clinical context (typically age >40 years, significant smoking history or biomass fuel exposure, progressive dyspnoea). This patient has a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58, which is clearly below 0.70, confirming fixed (persistent) airflow obstruction characteristic of COPD. The key is that spirometry must be performed AFTER bronchodilator administration to ensure that the obstruction is not fully reversible (which would suggest asthma rather than COPD). Option A is incorrect because reduced FEV1 alone does not diagnose COPD; the FEV1 percentage predicted determines severity of COPD once the diagnosis is established, but the diagnostic criterion is the FEV1/FVC ratio, not FEV1 alone. Many conditions can reduce FEV1. Option C is incorrect; while this patient has some reduction in FVC, the FEV1/FVC ratio <0.70 indicates obstructive (not restrictive) disease. In restrictive disease, both FEV1 and FVC are reduced proportionally, maintaining a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.70). Option D is incorrect; while this patient does show some bronchodilator response (100mL improvement in FEV1), this is less than the threshold for significant reversibility (200mL AND 12% improvement), and more importantly, the persistent post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms COPD. Some COPD patients demonstrate partial bronchodilator reversibility, which does not exclude the diagnosis if the post-bronchodilator ratio remains <0.70. This patient has GOLD Grade 2 (moderate) COPD based on FEV1 58% predicted (GOLD 1: FEV1 ≥80%, GOLD 2: 50-79%, GOLD 3: 30-49%, GOLD 4: <30%). Management should include smoking cessation support (already achieved - reinforce this), influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, initiation of long-acting bronchodilator therapy (LAMA or LABA), pulmonary rehabilitation referral, and assessment for other comorbidities.
mcqs.summary: COPD diagnosis requires post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 on spirometry in appropriate clinical context (age >40, smoking/exposure history, progressive dyspnoea). Post-bronchodilator testing is essential to distinguish from asthma. FEV1 % predicted determines COPD severity (GOLD 1-4), not diagnosis.
citations: COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand) 2024: Section 2 - Diagnosis of COPD
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD - Diagnosis and Spirometry (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 68-year-old former smoker (40 pack-year history, ceased 2 years ago) attends Young District Hospital respiratory clinic following spirometry confirming COPD. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows: FEV1 1.4L (42% predicted), FVC 2.8L (68% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.50. She reports breathlessness walking on level ground requiring frequent stops, and has had 3 exacerbations in the past 12 months, two requiring oral corticosteroids and antibiotics, and one requiring hospital admission. Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea scale score is 3 (stops for breath after walking about 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground). She has no current exacerbation. On examination: appears mildly dyspnoeic at rest. Vital signs: BP 142/86 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 92% on room air. BMI 24 kg/m². Respiratory examination shows reduced breath sounds bilaterally with prolonged expiration.
question.stem: According to the GOLD (Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease) classification, which grade and group best describes this patient's COPD?

options.A: GOLD Grade 2 (Moderate), Group A (low risk, fewer symptoms)
options.B: GOLD Grade 3 (Severe), Group B (low risk, more symptoms)
options.C: GOLD Grade 3 (Severe), Group E (high risk, high exacerbation history)
options.D: GOLD Grade 4 (Very Severe), Group D (high risk, more symptoms)

mcqs.explanation: The GOLD classification system for COPD has two components: spirometric grade (based on FEV1 % predicted) and symptom/risk group. According to the COPD-X Guidelines 2024 incorporating the updated GOLD 2023 classification, this patient's spirometric grade is determined by post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 42% predicted, which falls into GOLD Grade 3 (Severe COPD): GOLD 1 (Mild) FEV1 ≥80%, GOLD 2 (Moderate) 50-79%, GOLD 3 (Severe) 30-49%, GOLD 4 (Very Severe) <30%. The GOLD 2023 update introduced a new Group E classification for patients with exacerbation history. The patient groups are now: Group A (0-1 exacerbations per year not requiring hospitalization, AND mMRC 0-1 or CAT <10), Group B (0-1 exacerbations per year not requiring hospitalization, AND mMRC ≥2 or CAT ≥10), and Group E (≥2 moderate exacerbations per year, OR ≥1 exacerbation requiring hospitalization). This patient has had 3 exacerbations in 12 months with one hospital admission, clearly meeting Group E criteria regardless of symptom score. The eTG Complete 2024-2025 notes that the Group E classification identifies patients at highest risk who require more intensive treatment, particularly triple therapy (ICS-LABA-LAMA). Option A is incorrect on both counts (FEV1 42% is Grade 3 not Grade 2, and 3 exacerbations with hospitalization is not Group A). Option B is incorrect as the high exacerbation frequency (3 in 12 months with hospitalization) makes the patient Group E, not Group B. Option D is incorrect; while the risk group could align with the older 'Group D' terminology, the spirometry shows GOLD 3 (FEV1 42%), not GOLD 4 (which requires FEV1 <30%). This patient requires escalation of therapy to triple therapy (ICS-LABA-LAMA combination), pulmonary rehabilitation, consideration of long-term macrolide therapy (azithromycin) to reduce exacerbations, oxygen assessment, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), and regular follow-up. The high exacerbation frequency despite being Group E indicates need for maximal medical therapy and possibly specialist respiratory review.
mcqs.summary: GOLD classification: spirometric grades 1-4 based on FEV1 % predicted (1:≥80%, 2:50-79%, 3:30-49%, 4:<30%). Symptom/risk groups: A (low exacerbations, low symptoms), B (low exacerbations, high symptoms), E (≥2 exacerbations/year OR ≥1 hospitalization - high risk requiring intensive treatment).
citations: COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand) 2024: Section 3 - GOLD Classification and Assessment
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD - Severity Classification and Risk Stratification (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 71-year-old man with known COPD (GOLD Grade 2, Group B) presents to Wagga Wagga Base Hospital Emergency Department with a 3-day history of worsening breathlessness, increased cough, and change in sputum. He reports that his sputum has increased in volume and changed from its usual white colour to yellow-green. He has increased his use of salbutamol from twice daily to 6-8 times daily but with minimal relief. He denies fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis. His usual medications are tiotropium 5 micrograms once daily and salbutamol as needed. He is an ex-smoker (ceased 5 years ago, 50 pack-year history). On examination: appears dyspnoeic at rest. Vital signs: BP 148/88 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 24/min, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.4°C. Respiratory examination reveals reduced air entry bilaterally, scattered wheeze, and coarse crepitations in the right lower zone. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no focal consolidation.
question.stem: According to the Anthonisen criteria, how would you classify this COPD exacerbation?

options.A: Type 1 (severe) exacerbation - all three cardinal symptoms present
options.B: Type 2 (moderate) exacerbation - two of three cardinal symptoms present
options.C: Type 3 (mild) exacerbation - one cardinal symptom plus other features
options.D: Not a true exacerbation - likely pneumonia given focal crepitations on examination

mcqs.explanation: The Anthonisen criteria are used to classify COPD exacerbations and guide antibiotic therapy. According to the COPD-X Guidelines 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, the three cardinal symptoms of COPD exacerbation are: (1) increased dyspnoea, (2) increased sputum volume, and (3) increased sputum purulence (change in colour to yellow or green, indicating bacterial infection). Anthonisen classification: Type 1 (severe) exacerbation has ALL THREE cardinal symptoms; Type 2 (moderate) has TWO of three symptoms; Type 3 (mild) has ONE cardinal symptom plus at least one of: upper respiratory tract infection within 5 days, fever without other cause, increased wheeze, increased cough, or increased respiratory rate/heart rate by 20% above baseline. This patient clearly demonstrates all three cardinal features: (1) increased dyspnoea (worsening breathlessness, increased reliever use, dyspnoea at rest), (2) increased sputum volume (explicitly stated), and (3) increased sputum purulence (change from white to yellow-green), making this a Type 1 (severe) exacerbation. The presence of all three symptoms, particularly sputum purulence, indicates likely bacterial infection and is an indication for antibiotic therapy in addition to bronchodilator escalation and corticosteroids. Option B would apply if only 2 of the 3 cardinal symptoms were present. Option C would apply with only 1 cardinal symptom. Option D is incorrect; while the focal crepitations raise consideration of pneumonia (and chest X-ray was appropriately performed), the absence of focal consolidation on CXR and the presence of classical exacerbation features make COPD exacerbation the primary diagnosis. The crepitations may represent retained secretions or concurrent infection. According to Australian guidelines, Type 1 exacerbations require: supplemental oxygen (target SpO2 88-92% in COPD), escalated bronchodilator therapy (nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium), oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 30-50mg daily for 5 days), and antibiotics (first-line: amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days, or doxycycline if penicillin allergy). This patient's SpO2 of 88% on air is acceptable for COPD (target 88-92%, as higher oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in some patients), but supplemental oxygen should be provided if SpO2 falls below 88%.
mcqs.summary: Anthonisen criteria for COPD exacerbations: Type 1 (all 3 cardinal symptoms - increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) requires antibiotics + corticosteroids + bronchodilators. Type 2 (2 symptoms) and Type 3 (1 symptom + other features) may not require antibiotics. Sputum purulence indicates bacterial infection.
citations: COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand) 2024: Section 5 - COPD Exacerbations and Anthonisen Criteria
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD Exacerbations - Assessment and Classification (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 65-year-old woman with COPD presents to Dubbo Base Hospital Emergency Department with an acute exacerbation. She reports 2 days of increased breathlessness and increased cough. Her sputum volume has increased slightly but remains white in colour (not purulent). She has no fever and denies any sick contacts. She has COPD GOLD Grade 2 (FEV1 65% predicted) with infrequent exacerbations (last exacerbation 18 months ago). On examination: appears mildly dyspnoeic. Vital signs: BP 135/82 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.8°C. Chest examination reveals bilateral wheeze and reduced air entry, no focal crepitations. Chest X-ray shows no consolidation. The emergency physician is considering whether to prescribe antibiotics as part of the exacerbation management.
question.stem: According to Australian COPD management guidelines, is antibiotic therapy indicated for this patient's exacerbation?

options.A: Yes, antibiotics should always be given for all COPD exacerbations to prevent bacterial complications
options.B: No, antibiotics are not indicated - this is likely a viral exacerbation without purulent sputum
options.C: Yes, but only if sputum culture confirms bacterial infection before starting therapy
options.D: Yes, empirical antibiotics should be started due to the increased breathlessness and SpO2 <92%

mcqs.explanation: According to the COPD-X Guidelines 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated for all COPD exacerbations. The decision to use antibiotics is based on the Anthonisen criteria and the presence of purulent sputum, which is the key indicator of bacterial infection. This patient has only ONE cardinal symptom (increased dyspnoea) without increased sputum purulence, classifying this as at most a Type 3 exacerbation (or possibly Type 2 if increased sputum volume is considered). The Australian guidelines are clear that antibiotics should be reserved for exacerbations with purulent sputum (indicating bacterial infection), specifically: (1) Type 1 exacerbations (all 3 cardinal symptoms including purulent sputum), or (2) Type 2 exacerbations if purulent sputum is one of the two symptoms present. The rationale is that many COPD exacerbations are viral or due to environmental factors (air pollution, allergens) and do not require antibiotics. Indiscriminate antibiotic use contributes to antimicrobial resistance without clinical benefit. In this case, the sputum remains white (non-purulent), strongly suggesting a non-bacterial cause (likely viral or inflammatory). Option A is incorrect and contradicts Australian guidelines; routine antibiotics for all exacerbations are not recommended. Option C is incorrect; waiting for culture results before starting antibiotics in genuine bacterial exacerbations would cause harmful delays. When antibiotics are indicated (purulent sputum), they should be started empirically based on clinical criteria, not culture results (cultures are rarely performed in outpatient exacerbations). Option D is incorrect; low SpO2 indicates severity of exacerbation but does not in itself indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics. Severe exacerbations can be viral or non-infectious. This patient should receive: supplemental oxygen if SpO2 <88% (target 88-92%), increased bronchodilator therapy (nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium), and oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 30-50mg daily for 5 days). The absence of purulent sputum means antibiotics are not indicated. The patient should be advised to return if sputum becomes purulent (yellow/green), fever develops, or symptoms significantly worsen.
mcqs.summary: Antibiotics in COPD exacerbations: only indicated if purulent sputum present (Type 1 or selected Type 2 Anthonisen exacerbations). Non-purulent exacerbations are typically viral/inflammatory - treat with bronchodilators + corticosteroids, NO antibiotics. Antibiotic overuse drives resistance without benefit.
citations: COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand) 2024: Section 5.3 - Antibiotic Therapy in COPD Exacerbations
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD Exacerbations - Antibiotic Indications (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 58-year-old man with COPD GOLD Grade 3 (FEV1 38% predicted) presents to Orange Health Service with an acute exacerbation meeting all three Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and purulent sputum). He has been commenced on supplemental oxygen (target SpO2 88-92%), nebulised bronchodilators (salbutamol and ipratropium), and antibiotics (amoxicillin 500mg three times daily). The medical registrar is now considering whether to add systemic corticosteroids to the treatment regimen. The patient has no contraindications to corticosteroids (no active diabetes, no active peptic ulcer disease, no severe osteoporosis). He has had 4 exacerbations in the past 12 months requiring medical treatment.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen for this COPD exacerbation according to Australian guidelines?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 30-50mg daily for 5 days (no taper required)
options.B: Oral prednisolone 50mg daily for 14 days with gradual taper over further 7 days
options.C: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100mg four times daily for 5 days
options.D: Inhaled budesonide 800 micrograms twice daily is sufficient, no oral corticosteroids needed

mcqs.explanation: According to the COPD-X Guidelines 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, systemic corticosteroids are recommended for moderate to severe COPD exacerbations as they reduce treatment failure, shorten recovery time, improve lung function and symptoms, and reduce hospital stay length. The recommended regimen is oral prednisolone 30-50mg daily (most commonly 30-40mg or 50mg) for 5 days, with NO tapering required for short courses of this duration. The evidence shows that 5 days of corticosteroids is as effective as longer courses (10-14 days) with fewer adverse effects, and that there is no benefit to tapering for courses under 2 weeks. Shorter courses minimize adverse effects including hyperglycaemia, increased infection risk, osteoporosis, and adrenal suppression. Option B (14 days with taper) represents outdated practice; longer courses are no more effective than 5 days but increase adverse effects significantly, particularly important in COPD patients who often have multiple comorbidities (diabetes, osteoporosis). The COPD-X Guidelines explicitly state that courses longer than 5-7 days are not recommended. Option C (IV hydrocortisone) is reserved for patients unable to take oral medications (severe respiratory distress, vomiting, altered consciousness) or requiring ICU admission. For patients able to swallow, oral prednisolone is preferred as it is equally effective, easier to administer, and has better patient compliance. If IV therapy is used, equivalent dosing would be hydrocortisone 100mg IV four times daily, but this patient can take oral therapy. Option D is incorrect; while inhaled corticosteroids are important for long-term COPD management (particularly in patients with frequent exacerbations), they are not adequate treatment for acute exacerbations. Systemic corticosteroids are required to manage the acute inflammatory response. This patient should receive prednisolone 30-50mg daily for 5 days alongside the already-commenced bronchodilators and antibiotics, with review of long-term therapy (likely requires escalation to triple therapy given GOLD Grade 3 with 4 exacerbations per year, placing him in Group E).
mcqs.summary: COPD exacerbations require oral prednisolone 30-50mg daily for 5 days (no taper needed for short courses <2 weeks). Five days is as effective as longer courses with fewer adverse effects. IV corticosteroids reserved for severe cases unable to take oral therapy. Start corticosteroids early in moderate-severe exacerbations.
citations: COPD-X Guidelines (Australian and New Zealand) 2024: Section 5.4 - Corticosteroid Therapy in COPD Exacerbations
eTG Complete - Respiratory: COPD Exacerbations - Systemic Corticosteroids (2024-2025)

question.scenario: A 67-year-old woman with newly diagnosed COPD (GOLD Grade 2, FEV1 68% predicted, Group A - low exacerbation risk, mMRC dyspnoea score 1) attends Young District Hospital respiratory clinic for initiation of maintenance therapy. She reports breathlessness walking uphill or climbing stairs, with no significant limitation on level ground. She has no history of exacerbations. She is an ex-smoker (ceased 3 years ago, 35 pack-year history). She currently uses salbutamol 100 micrograms as needed, approximately once daily. On examination today: appears well. Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 16/min, SpO2 95% on room air. Chest examination reveals quiet breath sounds bilaterally with prolonged expiratory phase, no wheeze currently.
question.stem: What is the most appropriate first-line maintenance bronchodilator therapy for this patient according to Australian COPD guidelines?

options.A: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) such as tiotropium 5 micrograms once daily
options.B: Long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) such as indacaterol 150 micrograms once daily
options.C: Combination LABA-LAMA such as indacaterol-glycopyrronium 110/50 micrograms once daily
options.D: Continue salbutamol as needed only, no long-acting bronchodilator required at this stage

mcqs.explanation: According to the COPD-X Guidelines 2024 and eTG Complete 2024-2025, long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) monotherapy is the preferred first-line maintenance bronchodilator for most patients with COPD who have persistent symptoms despite short-acting bronchodilator use. LAMAs such as tiotropium (5 micrograms once daily via Respimat, or 18 micrograms once daily via HandiHaler), glycopyrronium (50 micrograms once daily), or umeclidinium (62.5 micrograms once daily) provide 24-hour bronchodilation, improve lung function, reduce dyspnoea, improve quality of life, and reduce exacerbation risk. The evidence base for LAMA is particularly strong for exacerbation prevention, even in lower-risk patients. This patient has GOLD Grade 2 COPD with symptomatic limitation (mMRC 1 indicates 'breathless hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill') requiring regular maintenance therapy. Option B (LABA monotherapy) is also effective and can be used as first-line therapy, but Australian guidelines give preference to LAMA due to superior exacerbation prevention in head-to-head trials and once-daily dosing improving adherence. LABA options include indacaterol 150 micrograms once daily, or formoterol/salmeterol twice daily. If LABA is chosen first and symptoms persist, LAMA would be added (or vice versa). Option C (combination LABA-LAMA) is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms despite LAMA or LABA monotherapy, or for Group B/E patients (higher symptom burden or exacerbation risk). Starting with combination therapy in a Group A patient is not recommended as it increases cost and side effects without proven additional benefit over monotherapy at this stage. Step-up to combination can occur if monotherapy is insufficient after 4-8 weeks. Option D is inappropriate; this patient has persistent daily symptoms requiring reliever use daily and limitation of activities (dyspnoea on stairs), meeting criteria for initiation of long-acting bronchodilator therapy. Continuing SABA-only therapy would leave her symptoms suboptimally controlled and miss the opportunity to improve quality of life and reduce future exacerbation risk.
